19.1: 19.1 The burden of Egypt, etc. The same. It should be known that many things said here pertain to Egypt historically; but both here and in other places of the Scriptures many things are set down which cannot stand according to the history, so that we are compelled by the necessity of the matter to seek a higher understanding. Behold the Lord will ascend, etc. The same. Egypt, darkness or sorrow, etc., up to: 'and the hearts of the wise men of Egypt melted with fear.' The idols of Egypt. Idolatry, feeling itself broken, so that even the magi, taught by demons, or understanding according to the prophecy of Balaam that the Son of God had been born, who had destroyed the magic art, came to Bethlehem and adored the Child.
19.2: 19.2 And I will make to run together. The same. Whence in the Gospel: I came not to send peace upon the earth, but the sword: for I came to set a man at variance against his father, etc. (Matt. 10).
19.3: 19.3 And shall be broken, etc. The same. The will of Egypt will be divided into opposites, so that they no longer think great things as before, but, separated by the spiritual sword, know that their counsel has been precipitate.
19.4: 19.4 Of cruel lords. Egypt was handed over to many lords. First to the Assyrians, afterward to Nebuchadnezzar, third to Alexander, finally to the Romans, Antony and Cleopatra being conquered by Augustus. The Chaldeans were more cruel, the Romans more powerful.
19.5: 19.5 And shall dry up. It is wont to happen that when captivity comes by the wrath of God, pestilence follows His indignation, and the elements rage against sinners. When, therefore, captivity came through the Chaldeans or Romans, perhaps both the Nile and the springs were dried up. Hyperbolically also, because of excessive tribulation, the rivers can be said to have failed and the springs and streams to have dried.
19.11: 19.11 Fools. When the Babylonian or Roman captivity came, all the counsels of the magi failed. The princes of Tanis. JEROME. Of humble command; for all heretics teach humility contrary to height, and drag down to the lower world, and the princes were of humble command and cast down. The son of the wise. Everyone used to say this to Pharaoh, etc., up to: 'and they boast that the great gods, Isis and Osiris and Typhon, were the founders of their nation.' Of ancient kings. As if he said: I have knowledge of the Scriptures with worldly wisdom.
19.14: 19.14 Drunk and vomiting. The same. With the fury of dragons, so that at last after vomiting they may understand their drunkenness. For as long as they are drunk, they will have neither beginning nor end.
19.15: 19.15 Restraining. HAYMO on Isaiah. Instead of what Jerome ought to have translated, etc., up to: 'others, from wantonness, know not what they do.'
19.16: 19.16 Women. Whom Egypt loves, whom alone Pharaoh wants to live, the men being killed. The devil kills the virtues, preserves the vices.
19.17: 19.17 The land of Judah to Egypt. The knowledge of the Scriptures, the law and the prophets; the Gospels will be a feast to Egypt when it has known itself, or a terror when it has understood that it had lies. For a dread. Others, for a feast, etc., up to: 'by promising them help.'
19.18: 19.18 Five cities. Some understand the five books of Moses, etc., up to: 'because they are changed from vices to virtues.' The language of Canaan. The question is why not the Hebrew language, etc., up to: 'and those who delight in unclean touch.'
19.19: 19.19 In that day. The same. Onias the priest, not understanding this, etc., up to: 'and that they have kept their own language to this day.' And a monument. The monument of the Lord is the evangelical and apostolic doctrine, which extends to the ends of the earth, whence: Their sound has gone forth into all the earth (Ps. 18). Or the monument by the boundary of faith is good work, which should extend as far as faith does, or the imitation of the Passion of Christ.
19.20: 19.20 For they shall cry. When the evangelical doctrine has grown, and persecution has come upon them, then those who have believed will cry to God the Father.
19.23: 19.23 In that day. Before the coming of the Lord, the individual nations, etc., up to: 'who run from kingdom to kingdom.' And the Egyptians shall serve. Not that afterward they would be subjugated, etc., up to: 'of the same condition with them.' In that day shall be. The same. He will not in turn be harassed in the middle by the Assyrians and Egyptians, but will be a third serving with them, namely the Romans.
19.25: 19.25 Blessed. These regions had abounded above all other monarchies, and therefore deserved to be blessed.
20.1: 20.1 In the year. The same. These are Assyrian names, etc., up to: 'he attacks those who serve generation and lust.' In the year. Ashdod, the most powerful city of the Philistines of the five, etc., up to: 'which the Lord spoke through him.' When he had sent. Beautifully, the king of the Assyrians is called Sargon, that is, prince of gardens, to whom Ahab is similar: who desired to turn the vineyard of Naboth into a garden; which he, understanding tropologically, preferred to die rather than do, lest his paternal inheritance and ancient possession be changed into the delights of an impious king.
20.2: 20.2 Go and loose. The prophet is commanded to lay aside sackcloth and shoes, etc., up to: 'for nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed.' And he did so. Wonderful obedience: a man of the highest nobility, as the Hebrews relate, went clothed only in haircloth. King Manasseh took his daughter in marriage; he was not ashamed to go naked, judging nothing more honorable than to obey the Lord.
20.3: 20.3 Barefoot. The same. It should be noted that before Ashdod is taken, etc., up to: 'to which he hastens, either to stand or to walk.'
20.4: 20.4 To shame. Because they could not eat the Passover of the Lord, which is eaten with loins girded, a staff in hand, feet shod, so that, passing through the solitude of this world, one may not be bitten by serpents.
20.6: 20.6 Was this. The wonderful providence of God, etc., up to: 'at the end it will perish entirely, when the kingdom of Christ shall have shone forth.'
21.1: 21.1 The burden of the desert of the sea. Of Babylon, called a sea for the multitude of its people. It comes from the desert. In which the Lord was tempted, in which the Israelites were struck by serpents.
21.2: 21.2 He that is unbelieving. A general sentence, as if it is the fault of individuals that they are crushed in the storm. Go up, Elam. The Septuagint: Elamites and ambassadors of the Persians. Elamites, despising. Go up, as if he said: O Persians and Medes, do not fear, mount your horses, besiege Babylon. Go up. Trusting in the strength of God, he speaks boldly against his adversaries. All the sighing. By which it made you and other nations sigh; or, that no one may now sigh, oppressed by the power of Babylon; or, that she be so afflicted with evils that she dare not sigh against you.
21.5: 21.5 Prepare the table. As if he said: O Persians and Medes, take food, etc., up to: 'in which you may restrain the fiery darts of the devil.' Behold, etc. What may follow the table, or, behold, O Belshazzar, what is written on the wall: Mene, Tekel, Peres.
21.6: 21.6 A watchman. The prophets are called watchers.
21.7: 21.7 A rider. Cyrus the prince ruled the Medes and Persians, etc., up to: 'the letter and the spirit, they refer to the two Testaments.'
21.8: 21.8 A lion. The same lion for strength of mind, who is the watchman by the prerogative of contemplation. Upon the watchtower of the Lord. That is, set in contemplation by day, ready by day and night to hear and to speak what He shall command. Standing all the nights. That I may guard myself from every sin, that I may be worthy to hear the word of the Lord.
21.9: 21.9 Behold, this man comes. What follows signifies that he has seen the Savior coming, sitting on a chariot with two animals, that is, an ass and a camel, yoking one chariot. It has fallen, it has fallen. When Cyrus and Darius laid Babylon waste, the idols too were broken, the temple of Bel being overthrown and burned with fire.
21.10: 21.10 My threshing. As if He said: O people, who are to be stored in my barns, whom I have threshed with various straits to shake out the chaff and bring the pure wheat into the barns, what I have heard from the Lord, the God of Israel, etc.
21.11: 21.11 The burden of Dumah. The Septuagint: of Idumea, etc., up to: 'the burden of Dumah cries to me.' He cries to me. JEROME. God, namely my keeper, etc., up to: 'then he speaks to the Gentiles: If you seek me, seek more earnestly (John 9).'
21.12: 21.12 The morning comes, etc. As to my people I will give the light of gladness, etc., up to: 'by work, and so I shall hear you.'
21.13: 21.13 The burden in Arabia. The Arabs are Saracens, etc., up to: 'thence God addresses the Jews fleeing thus: In the forest in the evening. O Jews, who will flee the Babylonian siege, you will sleep in the forest, that is, in the woods of the Saracens, fleeing the Chaldeans, in the paths of Dedanim, which is interpreted 'among neighbors' or 'kinsmen,' that is, on the road which leads to your kinsmen the Saracens.' Evening. The same. Which is the beginning of night. He who begins to sin is in the evening; he who reaches the height, in midnight. At midnight the firstborn of Egypt are killed. Peter denies; when daylight is near he repents. In the paths. The same. Because the evening is the beginning of evils, etc., up to: 'when he rebelled against his father.'
